The salt pans of the Ria de Aveiro

The pans are shallow rectangles of clay, laid out between the channels of the
lagoon, and they have been worked in the same shape since the tenth century. A
pan is not a machine and it is not a field. It is a slow instrument that reads
the weather, and the person who works it does almost nothing except decide when
water moves from one rectangle to the next.

Water enters from the lagoon at the high tide of a spring tide, through a gate
that the marnoto opens with a plank and a length of rope. From that moment the
water never runs uphill again. It falls through a sequence of rectangles, each
one shallower and warmer than the one before it, and in every rectangle it
leaves behind something it can no longer carry. The first rectangles are wide
and deep, and they are called the reservoirs; they hold three or four days of
supply and they drop the mud. The middle rectangles are the heaters, and their
only work is to raise the temperature of the water by four or five degrees,
which is the difference between a pan that crystallises in August and a pan that
does not. The last rectangles, the crystallisers, are the size of a small room
and hold two centimetres of water, and it is there that the salt appears. The
whole descent is about thirty centimetres over two hundred metres, and it is cut
by hand with a wooden blade, because a metal blade would cut through the clay
floor and a hole in the floor loses a season. A marnoto who inherits a pan
inherits the floor above all, and the first thing an old marnoto shows a young
one is not where the salt forms but where the floor is thin. The sequence has
no valves and no pumps, so an error made at the top of it cannot be corrected
lower down; the only control anyone has is the gate at the lagoon and the small
wooden sluices between one rectangle and the next, and both of them can do
nothing but let water fall. A pan is therefore read backwards: what the
crystallisers are doing today was decided four days ago at the reservoirs, and a
marnoto who wants a different result next week changes something this afternoon.

Evaporation does the work, and evaporation is only ever as good as the week.

The salt that forms first is not the salt that is sold first. On a still
afternoon, when the surface of a crystalliser is flat and the air is dry, a film
forms on the water itself: crystals a millimetre across, held up by surface
tension, drifting slowly against the downwind edge. That film is flor de sal.
It is skimmed off the water with a flat wooden rake, in one pass, and it must be
taken the same afternoon, because the first breath of wind sinks it and once it
touches the floor it is ordinary salt. A crystalliser gives perhaps a kilogram
of it on a good day. Underneath, over five or six days, a crust grows on the
floor of the pan, and that crust is the coarse salt, harvested with a long
wooden hoe drawn towards the bank, lifted out wet, and piled in a white cone
that drains for a month before it is moved. One pan gives twenty or thirty
tonnes of coarse salt and a few hundred kilograms of flor de sal in a season,
and the flor de sal is worth more per kilogram than everything else the pan
produces.

A season runs from June to September, and it is decided by rain. Rain in the
crystallisers dissolves the crust and sends the water back down the sequence, so
a wet August costs the whole harvest and not a part of it. The marnoto watches
the sky rather than the water, and the decision that matters is when to close
the gate: too early and the reservoirs run dry in a hot week, too late and a
storm fills the pans with fresh water. There is no instrument for it. There is a
person who has watched that lagoon for forty years, and there is a plank.

The number of working pans fell from about two hundred and seventy in the
nineteen fifties to fewer than twenty by the end of the century. Nothing
dramatic happened. Salt from mines and from industrial evaporation arrived at a
fraction of the price, refrigeration removed the need to salt fish, and the
young people who would have inherited the floors went to work in Aveiro instead.
A pan that is not worked for two seasons stops being a pan: the banks slump, the
channels silt, the clay floor cracks, and the lagoon takes the rectangle back.
Restoring one costs more than building a new one would, if anyone still knew how
to build a new one, and the cost is mostly the months of a person who knows
which part of the floor is thin.

What brought some of them back was not salt. It was the flor de sal and the
birds. Avocets, black-winged stilts and dunlin feed in a worked pan and not in a
drowned one, because the worked pan holds the shallow brackish water and the
small crustaceans that live in it, and a lagoon with no pans has none of that
habitat left. So the pans are now kept for two reasons that have nothing to do
with each other, and the person on the bank with the wooden rake is maintaining
a bird reserve as a side effect of skimming a film of crystals off two
centimetres of water.

The tools have not changed and there is a reason beyond tradition. Wood does not
taint the salt, it does not scar the floor, and a broken wooden rake is repaired
on the bank in an afternoon by the person who broke it. Every part of the
instrument can be rebuilt by its user from materials that are already there.
That is not nostalgia; it is the only property that let a technology survive a
thousand years in a place where nobody was coming to help.
